1.q: הַאֲזִ֥ינוּ הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֖יִם וַ⁠אֲדַבֵּ֑רָה וְ⁠תִשְׁמַ֥ע הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ אִמְרֵי־פִֽ⁠י
1.note: These two phrases **Listen, heavens, and let me speak** and **let the earth hear the utterances of my mouth** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See the introduction to this chapter for more information on parallelism. Alternate translation: [Listen to me, heavens and earth, as I speak]

Moses is referring to all of creation by naming two extremes, **heavens** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Listen, everything created] or [Hear, everything that exists]

2.q: יַעֲרֹ֤ף כַּ⁠מָּטָר֙ לִקְחִ֔⁠י תִּזַּ֥ל כַּ⁠טַּ֖ל אִמְרָתִ֑⁠י כִּ⁠שְׂעִירִ֣ם עֲלֵי־דֶ֔שֶׁא וְ⁠כִ⁠רְבִיבִ֖ים עֲלֵי־עֵֽשֶׂב
2.note: Moses is making comparisons between his teaching and various forms of water. The point of this comparison is that just as **rain** and **dew** are gentle and life-giving for plants, so is Moses’ **teaching** for the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Let my teaching be gentle and life-giving like rain, my words refreshing like dew, like gentle rain sprinkling on the green plants, and like showers that help the grass grow]

2.q: יַעֲרֹ֤ף כַּ⁠מָּטָר֙ לִקְחִ֔⁠י תִּזַּ֥ל כַּ⁠טַּ֖ל אִמְרָתִ֑⁠י כִּ⁠שְׂעִירִ֣ם עֲלֵי־דֶ֔שֶׁא וְ⁠כִ⁠רְבִיבִ֖ים עֲלֵי־עֵֽשֶׂב
2.note: These phrases mean basically the same thing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [Let my teaching fall gently and nourish you like life-giving water]

2.q: תִּזַּ֥ל כַּ⁠טַּ֖ל אִמְרָתִ֑⁠י כִּ⁠שְׂעִירִ֣ם עֲלֵי־דֶ֔שֶׁא וְ⁠כִ⁠רְבִיבִ֖ים עֲלֵי־עֵֽשֶׂב
2.note: Here Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [let my saying mist like dew, let my teaching be like sprinkling on the green plants, and let my saying be like downpours on the grass]

3.note: Here Moses is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is and to refer to Yahweh’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself] or [the character of Yahweh]

4.note: Here Moses is speaking of God as if he were a high **Rock** that they could climb up to reach safety from danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God, who is like a rock] or [God, who protects us like a rock]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because] or [since]

Here Moses is speaking of how God acts as if that were **ways** or paths that he was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his actions]

The terms **righteous** and **upright** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [completely righteous]

5.note: The pronoun **He** refers to Israel, while the pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel acted corruptly toward Yahweh]
Here Moses is speaking of the people of Israel as Yahweh’s **sons**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are not his people]

The terms **perverse** and **crooked** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they are a thoroughly corrupt generation]

6.q: הֲ־לַ⁠יְהוָה֙ תִּגְמְלוּ־זֹ֔את עַ֥ם נָבָ֖ל וְ⁠לֹ֣א חָכָ֑ם הֲ⁠לוֹא־הוּא֙ אָבִ֣י⁠ךָ קָּנֶ֔⁠ךָ
6.note: Moses is using the question form for emphasis and rebuke. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You foolish and unwise people should not reward Yahweh this way! He is certainly your father, your shaper!]
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The terms **foolish** and **without wisdom** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very foolish people]

Here Moses is speaking of Yahweh as if he were their **father** and **shaper**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who is like a father to you, the one who formed you] or [your creator and protector]

The terms **made** and **established** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He brought you into existence]

7.q: זְכֹר֙ יְמ֣וֹת עוֹלָ֔ם בִּ֖ינוּ שְׁנ֣וֹת דּוֹר־וָ⁠ד֑וֹר
7.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [Remember the days of eternity, yes, consider the years of generation upon generation]

Moses is using the terms **days** and **years** to refer to past events and experiences. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the events of ancient times, consider what happened to generation upon generation]

7.q: שְׁאַ֤ל אָבִ֨י⁠ךָ֙ וְ⁠יַגֵּ֔דְ⁠ךָ זְקֵנֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠יֹ֥אמְרוּ לָֽ⁠ךְ
7.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [Ask your father and your elders, and they will inform you]

8.note: Here Moses uses the phrase **gave the nations an inheritance** as if God were distributing property to his heirs, in order to describe how God assigned each nation its territory to live in. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When the Most High assigned the nations their territories] or [When the Most High gave each nation its place to live]
Moses is using the term **sons of man** to mean all of humanity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of people in the world]

Most ancient manuscripts read “sons of Israel.” The ULT follows that reading. One ancient manuscript reads “sons of God” which refers to heavenly beings. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [the sons of God] or [the angels of God]

9.q: חֵ֥לֶק יְהֹוָ֖ה עַמּ֑⁠וֹ יַעֲקֹ֖ב חֶ֥בֶל נַחֲלָתֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: Here Moses is speaking as if the people of Israel were **the portion of Yahweh** and **the portion of his inheritance**. He means that Yahweh chose Israel to be his special people, just as a person would choose a portion of land to be his own property. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh chose his people as his own, Jacob as his special possession]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel] or [the descendants of Jacob]

10.note: Here the pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh and **him** refers to Jacob (Israel). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh found Jacob] or [Yahweh found Israel]

10.q: יִמְצָאֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִדְבָּ֔ר וּ⁠בְ⁠תֹ֖הוּ יְלֵ֣ל יְשִׁמֹ֑ן
10.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by connecting the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [He found him in a wilderness land which was a barren, howling desert]

Moses is speaking of the **desert** as if it were a living thing that could howl. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in the barren desert where the wind howls] or [and in the barren, desolate desert]

The expressions **surrounded him** and **gave mind to him** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He carefully protected him]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person protects **the little man of his eye** (that is the pupil, or the apple of the eye) carefully, so Yahweh watched over his people carefully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [very carefully] or [with great care, as someone protects his own eye]

11.q: כְּ⁠נֶ֨שֶׁר֙ יָעִ֣יר קִנּ֔⁠וֹ עַל־גּוֹזָלָ֖י⁠ו יְרַחֵ֑ף יִפְרֹ֤שׂ כְּנָפָי⁠ו֙ יִקָּחֵ֔⁠הוּ יִשָּׂאֵ֖⁠הוּ עַל־אֶבְרָתֽ⁠וֹ
11.note: Here Moses is making a comparison between Yahweh and an eagle. The point of this comparison is that just as **an eagle** trains and protects its young, so Yahweh trained and protected Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly as is modeled in the UST.
A **pinions** refers to the outer flight feathers of a bird’s wing. If your readers would not be familiar with what pinions are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [his wings]

12.note: The pronoun **him** refers back to “his people, Jacob” from verse 9. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh alone led his people, Jacob]

13.q: וַ⁠יֹּאכַ֖ל תְּנוּבֹ֣ת שָׂדָ֑י וַ⁠יֵּנִקֵ֤⁠הֽוּ דְבַשׁ֙ מִ⁠סֶּ֔לַע וְ⁠שֶׁ֖מֶן מֵ⁠חַלְמִ֥ישׁ צֽוּר׃ חֶמְאַ֨ת בָּקָ֜ר וַ⁠חֲלֵ֣ב צֹ֗אן עִם־חֵ֨לֶב כָּרִ֜ים וְ⁠אֵילִ֤ים בְּנֵֽי־בָשָׁן֙ וְ⁠עַתּוּדִ֔ים עִם־חֵ֖לֶב כִּלְי֣וֹת חִטָּ֑ה וְ⁠דַם־עֵנָ֖ב תִּשְׁתֶּה־חָֽמֶר
13.note: Moses uses a repetitive series of clauses to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

Moses is using the past tense to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that the event will certainly happen. While the perspective of the entire song is from a future singer, in the time frame of Deuteronomy 32 the song here shifts from looking back at the Israelites’ ancestors to looking to the future at their descendants (in verses 13–21). If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense in verses 13–21. Alternate translation: [He will cause him to ride on heights of the land]

Here Moses is speaking of giving Israel control of the strategic, elevated parts of the land as if he were physically causing him to **ride on heights of the land**. This is an image for giving them victory and security. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gave him control of the high places of the land] or [He made him victorious over the land’s strongholds]

Here Moses is speaking as if Yahweh were physically nourishing them with **honey** from the **crag** or rocky cliff and **oil from the flinty stone**. This image describes miraculous abundance in a land so fertile that it provides these valuable foods even in the most unlikely places. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with honey even from the rocky places, and olive oil even from the stony ground]

14.note: Here, **fat** represents the best and richest part of the lambs and the wheat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the best of the lambs … the finest wheat]

Moses is using the possessive form to describe **rams** that are characterized by being from **Bashan**. Since Bashan was a region known for its excellent livestock, Moses is speaking of the rams as if they were the offspring of that land. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and rams from the region of Bashan] or [and rams from Bashan]

Here Moses is speaking of wine as if it were **the blood of grapes**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you drank wine made from grapes]

15.note: **Jeshurun** is a poetic name for the nation of Israel. The name means “the upright one,” but its use here is ironic since the verse describes Israel’s rebellion against God. Alternate translation: [Israel]

Here Moses uses the terms **fattened** and **kicked** to speak of Israel (here called Jeshurun) as if it were a well-fed animal that has become stubborn and rebellious. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Israel became prosperous and rebelled]

The terms **fat**, **thickened**, and **gorged** mean similar things. Moses is using the terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [you were obese]

15.q: שָׁמַ֖נְתָּ עָבִ֣יתָ כָּשִׂ֑יתָ וַ⁠יִּטֹּשׁ֙ אֱל֣וֹהַ עָשָׂ֔⁠הוּ וַ⁠יְנַבֵּ֖ל צ֥וּר יְשֻׁעָתֽ⁠וֹ
15.note: In this verse, the pronouns shift between **you** (referring to the Israelites) and **he** and **his** (also referring to the Israelites). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites were fat, the Israelites thickened, the Israelites gorged—and the Israelites abandoned the God who made them, and the Israelites rejected the Rock of their salvation]

Here Moses is speaking of God as if he were a high **Rock** that they could climb up to reach safety from danger. The point of this comparison also brings out that God is the strong and reliable source of their **salvation**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this in 32:4. Alternate translation: [the God who saves them powerfully] or [their strong Savior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the Rock who saved him] or [the Rock who saves]

16.note: The pronouns **He** and **their** refer to the Israelites, while the pronouns **him** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The Israelites provoked Yahweh with strangers. With their abominations they angered Yahweh]

Here, **strangers** represents the foreign gods that the Israelites began to worship. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with foreign gods]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [With their detestable practices] or [With what they did that was disgusting to God]

17.note: Here Moses is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestors]

18.q: צ֥וּר יְלָדְ⁠ךָ֖ תֶּ֑שִׁי וַ⁠תִּשְׁכַּ֖ח אֵ֥ל מְחֹלְלֶֽ⁠ךָ
18.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [You neglected the Rock, your bearer, indeed, you forgot the God who gave you birth]

Here Moses is speaking of God as if he were a high **Rock** that they could climb up to reach safety from danger. This image also emphasizes that God is strong, stable, and reliable like a rock. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God, who is strong and reliable]

Here Moses is speaking of God as if he were their **bearer** that **gave … birth** to the Israelites like a mother. This image refers to God as Creator who also established them as a nation. Your language may have comparable expressions that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your creator … the God who created you]

19.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh saw what they were doing and he spurned them]

Here Moses is speaking as if the Israelites were Yahweh’s **his sons and his daughters**. He means that they are his people, whom he chose and cared for. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his people]

20.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And he said that he would hide]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were physically going to **hide** his **face** from the Israelites. He means that he will withdraw his favor and protection from them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let me withdraw my favor from them] or [Let me stop protecting them]

Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were **children**. He means that his people are immature and unreliable in their relationship with him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people who are completely unreliable] or [people who cannot be trusted at all]

21.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [They made me jealous with a not-god, indeed, they angered me by their worthless things]

21.q: וַ⁠אֲנִי֙ אַקְנִיאֵ֣⁠ם בְּ⁠לֹא־עָ֔ם בְּ⁠ג֥וֹי נָבָ֖ל אַכְעִיסֵֽ⁠ם
21.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [so I will make them jealous with a not-people, indeed, I will anger them by a foolish nation]

22.note: Yahweh is using **a fire flares in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “my anger is very intense.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am extremely angry]

22.q: וַ⁠תִּיקַ֖ד עַד־שְׁא֣וֹל תַּחְתִּ֑ית וַ⁠תֹּ֤אכַל אֶ֨רֶץ֙ וִֽ⁠יבֻלָ֔⁠הּ וַ⁠תְּלַהֵ֖ט מוֹסְדֵ֥י הָרִֽים
22.note: Yahweh says **burns to the lowest Sheol, and devours the earth and its yield, and scorches the foundations of the mountains** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [burns with complete destruction and consumes everything thoroughly]

23.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [I will bring disaster after disaster upon them, yes, I will use up all my arrows against them]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his judgments were **arrows** that he would shoot from a quiver until they were all used up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will use all my judgments against them]

24.q: מְזֵ֥י רָעָ֛ב וּ⁠לְחֻ֥מֵי רֶ֖שֶׁף וְ⁠קֶ֣טֶב מְרִירִ֑י
24.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they will be wasted by hunger and weakened by plague and bitter contagion]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hunger**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by starving] or [by being hungry]

The expression **weakened by plague and bitter contagion** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and plague and bitter contagion weakening them] or [and becoming weak from plague and bitter contagion]

The terms **plague** and **bitter contagion** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [by deadly diseases] or [by severe pestilence]

Here, **the teeth of beasts** represents attacks by wild animals, and **the poison of crawlers in the dust** represents attacks by venomous snakes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and wild animals and venomous snakes will attack them]

The term **crawlers in the dust** refers to creatures that move along the ground, likely venomous snakes or similar reptiles. If your readers would not be familiar with this description, you could use a more general term or explain it. Alternate translation: [venomous snakes] or [poisonous reptiles that move along the ground]

25.note: Here, **sword** represents warfare or military attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Outside warfare will bereave] or [Outside military attack will bereave]

Here the author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and in the bedrooms, there will be terror]

26.note: If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [“I will wipe them out. I will remove from mankind their memory.”]

The meaning of this phrase in Hebrew is unclear. It may read **I would wipe them out**. The ULT follows that reading. The Hebrew verb may also mean “I would sweep them away” or “I would cut them to pieces.” Other ancient Greek manuscripts read “I would scatter them.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Moses is speaking of destroying the Israelites completely as if he were physically **wiping them out** like someone wiping away dirt or dust. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would destroy them completely] or [I would remove them entirely]

Here, **their memory** represents the remembrance of them by other people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the memory of them] or [all remembrance of them]

27.note: Moses is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what Moses is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [but I feared the provocation of the enemy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **provocation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the enemy provoking me]

The author is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives a reason for not completely destroying Israel so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that their adversaries would not misjudge, so that they would not say, “Our hand is exalted]

27.q: יֹֽאמְרוּ֙ יָדֵ֣י⁠נוּ רָ֔מָה וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְהוָ֖ה פָּעַ֥ל כָּל־זֹֽאת
27.note: There are three levels of quotation here. Moses is speaking (level 1) and quoting Yahweh (level 2) telling what the adversaries might say (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a third-level quotation. Alternate translation: [they say that their hand is exalted and that I did not carry out all this.’]

Here, **hand** represents power and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Our own power is great] or [We ourselves are strong]

28.q: כִּי־ג֛וֹי אֹבַ֥ד עֵצ֖וֹת הֵ֑מָּה וְ⁠אֵ֥ין בָּ⁠הֶ֖ם תְּבוּנָֽה
28.note: The pronouns **they** and **them** may refer either to the Israelites or to their enemies. The ambiguity may be intentional. If it is possible to maintain this ambiguity in your language, you may wish to do so. However, if you must clarify the reference and the context of your translation suggests the enemies are in focus, you could indicate this. Alternate translation: [For those nations are devoid of counsel, and without understanding in them]

28.q: כִּי־ג֛וֹי אֹבַ֥ד עֵצ֖וֹת הֵ֑מָּה וְ⁠אֵ֥ין בָּ⁠הֶ֖ם תְּבוּנָֽה
28.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [For they are a nation devoid of counsel, indeed, they are without understanding]

28.q: ג֛וֹי אֹבַ֥ד עֵצ֖וֹת הֵ֑מָּה וְ⁠אֵ֥ין בָּ⁠הֶ֖ם תְּבוּנָֽה
28.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **counsel** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [a nation that does not know how to plan wisely, and they are not able to understand]

29.note: Moses is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that the nations do not understand what will happen to them. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [Since they are not wise, they do not comprehend this] or [They are not wise, so they do not comprehend this]

30.q: אֵיכָ֞ה יִרְדֹּ֤ף אֶחָד֙ אֶ֔לֶף וּ⁠שְׁנַ֖יִם יָנִ֣יסוּ רְבָבָ֑ה אִם־לֹא֙ כִּי־צוּרָ֣⁠ם מְכָרָ֔⁠ם וַֽ⁠יהוָ֖ה הִסְגִּירָֽ⁠ם
30.note: Moses is using the question form to challenge his audience to recognize that Israel’s defeat by its enemies could only happen if God allowed it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [One could not chase a thousand, or two put ten thousands to flight, unless their Rock sold them and Yahweh gave them up!]
See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [unless their Rock, that is Yahweh, sold them, even gave them up]

Here Moses is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **Rock** that they could climb up to reach safety from danger and that would be a protection for the Israelites. He is then speaking as if God’s allowing the Israelites to be defeated were the same as if he **sold** them to their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unless Yahweh, who protects them like a rock, had allowed them to be defeated]
See how you translated the similar expression in verse 4.

31.note: Moses is speaking of God as if he were a high **Rock** that they could climb up to reach safety from danger. He also uses this image of the false gods of the enemies as if they were a **rock** that those people look to for protection. The point of the comparison is to show the vast difference in power and reliability between Yahweh and the false gods. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our God is far more powerful and reliable than their gods]

32.q: כִּֽי־מִ⁠גֶּ֤פֶן סְדֹם֙ גַּפְנָ֔⁠ם וּ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁדְמֹ֖ת עֲמֹרָ֑ה עֲנָבֵ֨⁠מוֹ֙ עִנְּבֵי־ר֔וֹשׁ אַשְׁכְּלֹ֥ת מְרֹרֹ֖ת לָֽ⁠מוֹ׃ חֲמַ֥ת תַּנִּינִ֖ם יֵינָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠רֹ֥אשׁ פְּתָנִ֖ים אַכְזָֽר
32.note: Moses is speaking of Israel’s enemies using poetic images that build from the source, **vine**, to the finished product, **wine**. He compares their gods to **the vine of Sodom** and **the vineyards of Gomorrah**, which produce **grapes** and **clusters** (people) that are poisonous and bitter, and finally **wine** (actions or delight in actions) that is like **the venom of serpents** and **the cruel poison of vipers**. It would be good to try to maintain this building or layering in your language if it would have the same effect.
See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [For their vine comes from Sodom, even from the vineyards of Gomorrah]

Moses is speaking of the enemies’ gods as if they were the **vine** and **vineyards** that produced poisonous fruit. He means that worshiping these gods lead to destructive and evil outcomes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For their gods are like vines from Sodom and vineyards from Gomorrah] or [For their gods come from wickedness like Sodom and Gomorrah]
See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [their grapes are poisonous, indeed the whole grape cluster is bitter]

Moses is speaking of the Israelites’ enemies as if they were **grapes** and **clusters** that were poisonous and bitter. He means that these enemies are corrupt and destructive in their character and actions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable figure of speech or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their deeds are corrupt and destructive] or [they are poisonous and bitter in their character]

32.q: כִּֽי־מִ⁠גֶּ֤פֶן סְדֹם֙ גַּפְנָ֔⁠ם וּ⁠מִ⁠שַּׁדְמֹ֖ת עֲמֹרָ֑ה עֲנָבֵ֨⁠מוֹ֙ עִנְּבֵי־ר֔וֹשׁ אַשְׁכְּלֹ֥ת מְרֹרֹ֖ת לָֽ⁠מוֹ
32.note: Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom, and their vine comes from the vineyards of Gomorrah; therefore their grapes are grapes of poison, and bitter clusters are what they produce]

33.q: חֲמַ֥ת תַּנִּינִ֖ם יֵינָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠רֹ֥אשׁ פְּתָנִ֖ים אַכְזָֽר
33.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [Their wine is as poisonous as the venom of serpents, indeed as deadly as the poison of vipers]

33.q: חֲמַ֥ת תַּנִּינִ֖ם יֵינָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠רֹ֥אשׁ פְּתָנִ֖ים אַכְזָֽר
33.note: Moses is speaking of the wickedness of the enemies of the Israelites as if it were the **venom of serpents** and **the cruel poison of vipers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Their wine is as deadly as the venom of serpents and the cruel poison of vipers] or [Their wine is like the venom of serpents and the cruel poison of vipers]

Here, **wine** represents what the enemies celebrate and take pleasure in. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What they celebrate is like the venom of serpents] or [They take pleasure in things as deadly as the venom of serpents]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the cruel poison of vipers is their wine]

34.note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is indeed concealed with me, sealed up among my treasures!]

The pronoun **it** refers to the judgment that Yahweh will bring, as clarified in the next verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Is not their punishment concealed with me]
This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, ‘Is it not]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his future plans for judgment as if they were a valuable document or object that is **sealed up** and kept safe **among** his **treasures** until the right time. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [safely stored and ready to use at the proper time] or [kept secure until I decide to act]

35.note: The terms **vengeance** and **recompense** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Vengeance is mine]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **vengeance** and **recompense**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [I am the one who will avenge and repay] or [I will punish and pay back]

Here the author is speaking of **the time when their foot slips** to mean a time when they would experience sudden calamity or failure. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when they suddenly fall into disaster] or [when calamity suddenly comes upon them]

35.q: כִּ֤י קָרוֹב֙ י֣וֹם אֵידָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠חָ֖שׁ עֲתִדֹ֥ת לָֽ⁠מוֹ
35.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [for the day of their disaster is near, yes, the things prepared for them hasten]

Here the author is speaking of **the things prepared for them** as if they were living things that could **hasten** or move quickly toward them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their doom is approaching rapidly]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. The word **for** gives the reason for the vengeance Yahweh described in verses 34–35. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

36.q: כִּֽי־יָדִ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עַמּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַל־עֲבָדָ֖י⁠ו יִתְנֶחָ֑ם כִּ֤י יִרְאֶה֙ כִּי־אָ֣זְלַת יָ֔ד וְ⁠אֶ֖פֶס עָצ֥וּר וְ⁠עָזֽוּב
36.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh seeing that his people’s strength is gone before the information about him having compassion on them, and put both of these before the information about him vindicating them. Alternate translation: [For Yahweh will see that gone is their hand, and there are none, kept back or let free. And he will have compassion on his servants and will vindicate his people]

36.q: כִּֽי־יָדִ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עַמּ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠עַל־עֲבָדָ֖י⁠ו יִתְנֶחָ֑ם כִּ֤י יִרְאֶה֙ כִּי־אָ֣זְלַת יָ֔ד וְ⁠אֶ֖פֶס עָצ֥וּר וְ⁠עָזֽוּב
36.note: The word translated as **For** at the beginning of the verse gives the reason why in verses 34–35 Yahweh described his vengeance. The second occurrence of **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came in the first part of the verse. Use connectors in your language that make these relationships clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh does all this to vindicate his people and he has compassion on his servants because he will see that gone is their hand, and there are none, kept back or let free]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and will act compassionately toward his servants]

Here, **hand** represents power and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their strength is gone] or [their power has failed]

Moses is referring to all of Yahweh’s people by naming two extremes, those who are **kept back** (confined or imprisoned) and those who are **let free** (at liberty). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [no one at all is left]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and there are none left, kept back] or [and there are none remaining, kept back]

37.q: אֵ֣י אֱלֹהֵ֑י⁠מוֹ צ֖וּר חָסָ֥יוּ בֽ⁠וֹ׃ אֲשֶׁ֨ר חֵ֤לֶב זְבָחֵ֨י⁠מוֹ֙ יֹאכֵ֔לוּ יִשְׁתּ֖וּ יֵ֣ין נְסִיכָ֑⁠ם
37.note: Yahweh is using the question form to taunt the people and their false gods, who are powerless to help them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Their gods are nowhere to be found—the rock in whom they took refuge, who ate the fat of their sacrifices, drank the wine of their libations!] or [Their gods cannot help them—the rock in whom they took refuge, who ate the fat of their sacrifices, drank the wine of their libations.]
See how you translated the similar expression in verse 31.

38.q: אֲשֶׁ֨ר חֵ֤לֶב זְבָחֵ֨י⁠מוֹ֙ יֹאכֵ֔לוּ יִשְׁתּ֖וּ יֵ֣ין נְסִיכָ֑⁠ם
38.note: Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He is speaking of the idols as if they were living beings **who ate the fat of their sacrifices** and **drank the wine of their libations**, when he really means that these idols are lifeless and powerless. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who never ate the fat of your sacrifices or drank the wine of your libations]

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But they will not rise up and help you; they cannot be protection for you]

Yahweh is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “take action” or “come to your aid.” He is not saying the false gods will literally stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let them come to your aid and help you] or [Let them take action and help you]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the false gods as if they were **a shelter** that could physically protect the Israelites. He means that these gods should be the ones to help and protect them, since the Israelites worshiped them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let them be the ones who protect you] or [let them keep you safe]

39.note: Here the pronoun **I** is repeated for emphasis, to make a very strong declaration of God’s unique identity. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself am he] or [I alone am he]

Here, **hand** represents God’s power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and no one rescues from my power] or [and no one can escape my control]

40.note: Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [You see,] or [Know that]

Lifting the **hand to heaven** was a symbolic action by which a person showed that they were swearing a solemn oath. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I swear a solemn oath]

Following the custom of his culture, God is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred, his own eternal existence. Alternate translation: [I swear by my eternal life] or [I vow by my own life, which lasts forever]

There are three levels of quotation here. Moses is speaking to the people (level 1) and quoting Yahweh (level 2) who is now quoting himself taking this oath (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a third-level quotation as modeled in the UST.

41.note: See the discussion on parallelism in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [I will punish my enemies, yes, I will pay back those who hate me]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his judgment as if it were a **sword**. The word **glittering** adds to the imagery of a fearsome weapon ready for use. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [my fearsome judgment, which is like a glittering sword] or [my terrible weapon of judgment]

Here Yahweh is speaking of **justice** as if it were a weapon or tool that his **hand** (representing his power) could take hold of in order to execute judgment. If this image communicates well in your language, you could use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I take hold of justice] or [and I am ready to execute justice]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he will **pay back** a debt. He means that he will punish those who hate him because they deserve punishment for the evil they have done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will punish those who hate me as they deserve]

42.q: אַשְׁכִּ֤יר חִצַּ⁠י֙ מִ⁠דָּ֔ם וְ⁠חַרְבִּ֖⁠י תֹּאכַ֣ל בָּשָׂ֑ר מִ⁠דַּ֤ם חָלָל֙ וְ⁠שִׁבְיָ֔ה מֵ⁠רֹ֖אשׁ פַּרְע֥וֹת אוֹיֵֽב
42.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the blood of the slain and the captives** with the information about **my arrows drunk with blood**. Similarly, you may want to put the information about **the heads of the leaders of the enemy** with the information about **my sword will devour flesh**. Alternate translation: [I will make my arrows drunk with the blood of the slain and the captives, and my sword will devour flesh from the heads of the leaders of the enemy]

42.q: אַשְׁכִּ֤יר חִצַּ⁠י֙ מִ⁠דָּ֔ם וְ⁠חַרְבִּ֖⁠י תֹּאכַ֣ל בָּשָׂ֑ר
42.note: Yahweh is speaking of his **arrows** and **sword** as if they were living things that could get **drunk** with blood and **devour** flesh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will use my arrows to kill so many people that it will be as if my arrows were drunk with blood, and I will use my sword to kill so many people that it will be as if my sword were devouring their flesh]

Yahweh is speaking of **the heads of the leaders** in a way that could have two meanings. This is poetic wordplay. The word **heads** could refer to the top-ranking leaders themselves, or it could refer to the literal heads of the enemy leaders that would be cut off. If your language has a way to preserve this ambiguity, you could do so. Alternatively, you could express one meaning, with the other in a footnote. Alternate translation: [from the severed heads of the enemy leaders] or [from the highest-ranking enemy leaders]

43.note: Moses is speaking to **nations** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s justice and vindication of his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the nations. Alternate translation: [Let the nations rejoice]

Some ancient manuscripts read **Nations, make his people rejoice**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Heavens, make his people rejoice, and all sons of God, worship him.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Here, **blood** represents the violent deaths of his servants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the violent deaths of his servants he will avenge]

Here Moses is speaking of Yahweh atoning for or purifying his land and people as if he will physically **cover** them. This image refers to removing the defilement of sin and bloodshed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will atone for his land and his people] or [and he will purify his land and his people]

44.note: The author is using the term **ears** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that the people could hear]

46.note: Moses is using the term **hearts** to represent the people’s attention and commitment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay close attention to all the words] or [Commit yourselves to all the words]

Moses is speaking of his testimony as if it were something that he physically **bore** or carried to the Israelites. He means that he has faithfully declared God’s message to them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have declared to you] or [I have testified to you]

Moses is using the term **words of this law** to represent what the law expresses by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all that this law says to do] or [everything that God has commanded in the law]

47.q: לֹֽא־דָבָ֨ר רֵ֥ק הוּא֙ מִ⁠כֶּ֔ם כִּי־ה֖וּא חַיֵּי⁠כֶ֑ם
47.note: Moses is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression, **empty**, that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [these instructions are extremely important for you, because obeying them will enable you to live well]
See how you translated the phrase “prolong your days” in 4:26. Alternate translation: [you may live for many years] or [you may have a long life]

48.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

49.note: **Mount Nebo** is the highest point of the northern part of the Abarim mountain range.

The author is using the expression **on the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “opposite” or “overlooking.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [opposite Jericho] or [overlooking Jericho]

50.note: Yahweh is using **gathered to your people** as a common expression of this culture to mean “join your ancestors in the place of the dead.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will join your ancestors in the place of the dead … and joined his ancestors in the place of the dead]

51.note: The words **Meribah** and **Kadesh** are the names of places, and **Zin** is the name of a wilderness region. You could add a footnote to show that this refers to the events described in Numbers 20:1–13.

52.note: Here, **from the front** represents being opposite to the land or in front of it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from a distance] or [from the opposite side]
